Tropical Update: Another short lived Tropical System is forming in the Northern Gulf, as of this morning the National Hurricane has initated advisories on Potential Tropical Cyclone 5 ( this just means the system is expected to become a Tropical Storm soon and has an immediate threat to land so they do this before it is offically a closed storm and a Tropical Depression/Storm to give folks a heads up) A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued for the northwestern Gulf Coast from Port Bolivar, Texas, to the Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line in Louisiana.

This system is showing signs of organization and should intensify into a Tropical Storm soon. The system is small, so while the official forecast only takes it to 45 MPH, I can't rule out it getting a little stronger. Small systems are sneaky and can sometimes strengthen faster than anticipated. The main concern will be the risk of heavy rainfall along parts of the upper Texas coast through east-central Texas and into far southwestern Louisiana Tuesday into Wednesday; some Flash Flooding is possible, especially in the Urban areas around Houston. Gusty winds are also possible. 

I'll pass along some updates as needed over the next 36 hours. 

-Ethan

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: HURRICANE TROPICAL MARIE EXPECTED TO DEVELOP - TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD REACH CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST⚠️🌀🌧️a developing tropical system well offshore of southwestern Mexico is expected to become Hurricane Marie this week, and it could eventually play an important role in the weather across California and the Southwest during the upcoming Labor Day weekend. The disturbance, currently designated EP95, now has an 80% chance of developing within 48 hours and a 90% chance within seven days. A tropical depression is likely to form within the next couple of days as the system moves generally west-northwest to northwest. Once Marie develops, the system is expected to eventually gain more of a north-to-northwestward component. This could allow tropical moisture associated with the storm to become drawn northward toward California and parts of the Southwest heading into Labor Day weekend. There is increasing confidence that indirect impacts will occur, particularly an increase in tropical moisture that could lead to higher humidity, more clouds and increased opportunities for showers and thunderstorms across parts of the region. Depending on exactly how the pattern evolves, locally heavy rainfall could also become a concern. However, it remains too early to determine whether Marie itself will produce any direct impacts in California or the Southwest. There is still considerable spread among the forecast models regarding the eventual track and how close the system could get to the region. Forecast uncertainty remains high, especially since the system has not developed a well-defined center yet. Until a consolidated circulation forms, models are essentially trying to forecast the future track of a center that does not fully exist. Confidence should begin to increase once the main center forms and models have a better starting point. This will be an important system to watch closely through the week as Labor Day weekend approaches⚠️🌀🌧️

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
🌡️ 4-Factor FeelsLike Forecast 🌡️ 
It’s the feels-like in Sun and Wind!
The US heat this week will be extreme. 
Traditional heat index forecasts do NOT include the sun and wind. Odd right? I’ve always thought they should because some folks spend so much time exposed. So, I found a formula from Dr. Robert Steadman in a white paper, and it turns out one version is being used by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology right now. This 4-factor equation I’m using takes both into account. Sun spikes it. In sunny spots the sun adds ~ 15°! Generally wind cools it. For instance: Nashville in the shade is 105. Raleigh in the shade feels like 102. DC in the shade is 100. Atlanta in the shade is 97. Bottom line you can NOT directly compare this to our NOAA traditional heat index, and it should not be used to replace it. It does illustrate how being in the summer Sun makes a dramatic difference. So… shade is your friend this week. Be safe!!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD SURGE INTO SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA NEXT WEEKEND🌴🌀🌧️ there are growing signals that tropical moisture could make a significant push northward into Southern California next weekend into early the following week, potentially bringing heavy rain, increased humidity, thunderstorms and strong south swells. A developing tropical disturbance off Mexico currently has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical cyclone within the next seven days. While it is far too early to know the eventual track or whether the tropical system itself gets anywhere near California, a notable number of ensemble and deterministic model solutions show the system - or a substantial plume of its moisture - being pulled northward from near Baja California toward Southern California. By next Sunday, the average precipitable water value among ensemble members climbs to around 1.5 inches, with several individual members exceeding 2 inches. Those would represent very high moisture levels for Southern California and could support periods of heavy rainfall if the necessary atmospheric lift develops. The evolving upper-level pattern will be critical. A cut-off low may linger near Northern California into the weekend, disrupting the typical subtropical ridge that often keeps tropical systems and their moisture confined farther south. If the trough remains near the West Coast, it could effectively open the door for tropical moisture to recurve northward toward California. There remains considerable uncertainty. Ensemble guidance still varies significantly regarding the position of the West Coast trough, the Southern Rockies ridge and the eventual tropical cyclone. Small changes in this pattern could mean the difference between deep tropical moisture reaching California or remaining largely offshore. For now, there is at least a chance of precipitation across Southern California next weekend, but confidence in exact rainfall amounts and locations remains low. This is not a forecast for a tropical cyclone landfall in California. The bigger concern at this stage is the possibility of a substantial tropical moisture surge producing heavy rain, thunderstorms, muggy tropical conditions and strong south swells. With roughly a week to go, expect plenty of changes in the forecast🌴🌀🌧️

All through late August, Venus has been creeping toward a distant blue-white star. Tonight, it arrives.

On September 1, Venus meets Spica in a close conjunction low in the west-southwest after sunset. The two make a striking odd couple: Venus, a planet just next door in cosmic terms, blazing as the Evening Star, and Spica, a searing binary star system some 250 light-years beyond it, its light having left before the telescope was even invented. Side by side, they look like near equals, yet Spica is millions of times farther away.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: FALL-LIKE STORM TO BRING RAIN, WIND & VERY HIGH-ELEVATION SNOW TO THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST THIS WEEK🌧️💨❄️a significant change to fall-like weather is increasingly likely across the Pacific NorthwestWednesday through Friday as a deep upper-level low and strong cold front move into the region. Widespread rain, gusty winds, much cooler temperatures and even some snow on the highest Cascade peaks are expected. Wednesday into Thursday currently looks like the wettest period, with widespread wetting rain likely from Washington through Oregon. The heaviest totals are favored along the coast, Coast Range, Olympics and Cascades. Parts of southwest Washington and northwest Oregon have a high likelihood of exceeding 1 inch of rain over a 48-hour period, with locally 2-3 inches or more possible in the higher terrain. Rainfall amounts will generally decrease farther inland, but rain should still reach portions of eastern Washington and Oregon. Showers linger into Friday. Gusty southerly winds will accompany the front Wednesday, particularly along the Washington and Oregon coasts, Northwest Interior and east of the Cascades. Some areas of eastern Washington could see gusts around 30-40 mph. While winds in western Washington may remain below typical advisory thresholds, impacts could be greater than the wind speeds alone suggest. Trees are still carrying full foliage, and some have been stressed by the dry summer, increasing the potential for isolated power outages and tree or branch damage. Much colder air will also arrive behind the front and with the upper low, with snow levels potentially falling to around 7,000 feet in the northern Washington Cascades Wednesday night and remaining relatively low through late week. This would mainly bring snow to the highest peaks rather than the mountain passes, but it will be another noticeable sign of the approaching seasonal transition. There will also be a low-end chance of thunderstorms across parts of the region Wednesday and Thursday. Any stronger showers or thunderstorms could produce brief heavy rain, lightning, small hail and locally gusty winds. Temperatures will tumble well below normal, with some areas running 10-20°F below normal. The rain may not completely end fire season, but widespread wetting rainfall and cooler conditions should provide meaningful relief and help slow ongoing wildfire activity🌧️💨❄️

items.text:
🌀 TROPICAL UPDATE: Chances are increasing for Tropical Storm #Edouard to briefly form in the Gulf early this week. I’m also watching the remnants of #Dolly. Here's the latest and what to know:

1) INVEST 97L: This is the area in the northern Gulf we are currently invest-igating (how it gets that Invest label). Today it has been getting its act together with increasing storm coverage and what appears to be a closed surface circulation. Right now, the NHC has bumped up development odds to 50% as of 2 PM Sunday, but respectfully, I feel that is too low based on recent observations. 

If trends continue, the Gulf could see a short-lived Tropical Depression or Tropical Storm #Edouard along with a cone here soon. Hurricane Hunters will be flying into the system starting Monday morning. In its projected path westward, water temperatures are warmer than average and wind shear will be pretty low, which would favor organization and strengthening. What will be working against the system will be dry air and time. It’ll be pushing onshore along the SE Texas or SW Louisiana coast on Tuesday. Even if it forms, it doesn’t appear to be a big or powerful storm, but ironically, smaller storms have historically shown that they can strengthen (or weaken) quickly. Impacts may be limited, but it'll still be capable of heavy rain / pockets of flooding, gusty wind, higher tides and even a tornado threat. 

2) REMNANTS OF DOLLY: Passing by Puerto Rico today and bringing scattered rain and storms to the area. They need every drop, 44% of the island is currently experiencing a Level 4 “Extreme” drought. The remnants of Dolly also brought winds gusts as high as 60 mph to the island of Saba in the Caribbean this morning. 

From here, it’ll head towards the direction of the Bahamas, Florida and Eastern Gulf. Florida timing would be Thursday, Friday…and even as late as the Labor Day weekend. I would think of it as Thursday (earliest) and Labor Day (latest) depending on track, which still has a big range. Biggest question that still needs to be answered is what will it approach as? Just a rainmaker with a lot of tropical moisture helping to increase rain chances? Or will it be a tropical system? Some models do show the potential for #Dolly to reform (it would still keep that name), but not all do. As a result, the current odds for development from the NHC are at 20% as of Sunday afternoon Regardless of what it becomes, Florida needs more rain!   

I'll continue to keep you updated 24/7 with no hype, just the facts. Thanks everyone!

- Matt Devitt Weather

What does “Ring of Fire” mean?

No, it doesn’t mean everything is literally on fire.

In weather, a “Ring of Fire” pattern happens when a large ridge of high pressure sets up and produces intense heat underneath it. Storm systems are often forced to travel around the outer edge of that heat dome, basically tracing a ring around it.

For us, the big story to start September looks to be the HEAT. Temperatures could soar well into the 90s and potentially near 100° at times during the first 10 days of the month.

The good news? These patterns eventually break down, and September is typically when we start watching for those first stronger pushes of cooler air.

So hang in there… summer isn’t finished with us just yet! 🥵

SEPTEMBER TORNADO AREAS:

September is the month where Fall begins to gain steam - although that will be delayed somewhat this year. The first sweeping cold fronts encounter deep gulf moisture and summer time instability still hanging around. We begin to see larger scale synoptic systems, again, meaning deeper lows/more organized cyclones. Thus, a large part of the lower 48 can experience tornadic activity. 

September is also peak waterspout month for the Great Lakes! The waters are still warm from summer, and we get those first cold pockets of air arriving from the north, thus making it the best combination of the two the entire year!

This coming September will be interesting, with our super El Nino being a major driving force behind out weather, we're not quite sure what to expect. Hurricanes that often bring increase tornado activity with them may not show up, and the heat dome may keep the ring of fire going longer than normal!

REMNANTS OF DOLLY - Thanks to strong wind shear, what’s left of Dolly no longer has a well-defined circulation, so it’s not a tropical storm anymore. It is, however, sending a welcome surge of tropical moisture across the drought-stricken northeastern Caribbean Islands and Puerto Rico.

High pressure building north of the system should steer the remnants over the Great Antilles or through the southern Bahamas and eventually into the southeastern Gulf later this week. Wind shear may relax somewhat along its path next week, but the chances of Dolly regenerating into a tropical depression or storm remain low. If it does manage a comeback, the Gulf would be the most likely place for it to happen.

GULF LOW PRESSURE - An area of low pressure about 125 miles south of the Louisiana coast is producing more concentrated showers and thunderstorms, but surface observations indicate the system hasn’t strengthened yet. Some slow development is possible over the next couple of days as it drifts toward the Louisiana and Texas coasts. Models bring the system ashore within about 2–3 days, which should put an end to any opportunity for tropical development.

And here’s the part I really like...

We’re now just 11 days away from the climatological peak of hurricane season on September 10, and there are no imminent tropical concerns anywhere!

items.author: GregDeeWeather

TROPICS | AUG 30 AM | The NHC has increased the chance for development both with the low in the Gulf & the remnants of Dolly. 

1. Invest 97L is the low-pressure system in the Gulf south of Mobile Bay. The system has a good amount of convection (thunderstorms) with it & a circulation, along with cloud banding that can be seen on satellite. All of this is a sign that it is organizing more, though the NHC says it has not yet strengthened. A tropical depression or tropical storm may form here over the next couple of days as the system drifts WNW toward Texas or Louisiana. 

Most of the models keep this as a weak system, but tropical storm strength is attainable before coming ashore. The main threat from systems like this is the flooding rain, which could in some places exceed 4-6" from the upper Texas coast into Louisiana. Anyone from Houston to New Orleans needs to monitor this system closely.

2. The remnants of Dolly are located in the Leeward Islands & are approaching Puerto Rico with heavy rain. The system will be experiencing some strong shear over the next day or so. As it approaches the Northwestern Bahamas & Florida, that shear will weaken. How much this strong shear impacts the storm will determine its chances farther northwest.

Although the chances are low, there is more than one model that suggests that Dolly's remnants may possibly try to regenerate once the system makes it somewhere near South Florida as a tropical wave. That may happen anywhere from the Northwest Bahamas to even the Eastern Gulf. Overall, the majority of the data still leans toward nothing else happening with this storm. But there are enough outliers for some redevelopment that we at least need to keep an eye on it. It looks like mid-week is around the time we'd need to start watching more closely for Florida & the Bahamas. 

I'll keep you updated.

items.text: TROPICAL MOISTURE BOOSTS RAIN CHANCES ACROSS CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST IN EARLY SEPTEMBER🌧️🌴🌀an active Eastern Pacific tropical pattern could become an important source of moisture for California and the Southwest during the first 7-10+ days of September, bringing multiple opportunities for increased clouds, showers and thunderstorms. Tropical Storm Karina is currently well southwest of Baja California and is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane, potentially becoming a major hurricane early next week. Karina itself is expected to remain well offshore, but moisture associated with the storm could become entrained into the broader atmospheric flow and pulled northeastward into Southern California and the Southwest. The first surge of tropical moisture could arrive as early as Tuesday into Wednesday. Confidence is high that Southern California will see an increase in mid-and high-level cloud cover, while confidence in measurable rainfall remains lower. Current forecasts generally show around a 30% chance of showers and thunderstorms Tuesday, with some of the better chances focused on Los Angeles and Ventura counties. Exactly how much moisture reaches California will depend heavily on Karina’s eventual track. A farther-west track would likely keep the deepest tropical moisture offshore, while a farther-east track could allow substantially more moisture to become involved and increase rainfall chances. Karina may not be the only tropical system worth watching. Longer-range guidance is already showing signals for another potential surge of tropical moisture into Southern California and the Southwest from a separate disturbance well south of southwestern Mexico. This system currently has a 90% chance of tropical development during the next seven days, with a tropical depression likely to form during the early or middle part of the week. Moisture associated with that system could potentially be drawn northward around September 7-9, bringing another opportunity for showers and thunderstorms - and possibly better rain chances than the moisture associated with Karina. There is still plenty of uncertainty regarding the exact tracks of these tropical systems and how much moisture ultimately gets pulled north. However, the overall pattern increasingly favors multiple opportunities for tropical moisture to reach California and the Southwest during the opening 7-10+ days of September🌀🌧️🌴

items.text: A major pattern change will bring a stretch of cool, wet and increasingly fall-like weather to the Pacific and Inland Northwest this week! Tuesday may begin relatively quiet, with scattered showers and an isolated thunderstorm possible, but a stronger system arrives Wednesday, bringing widespread rain, breezy winds and much cooler temperatures. Additional rounds of rain and scattered thunderstorms will continue Thursday, with showers potentially lingering into Friday and Saturday. The coast, Olympics, Coast Range and Cascades will receive the most rain. Many areas could see 1-3 inches, with locally higher totals possible in the mountains and foothills. Interior western Washington and Oregon may receive around 0.50-1.25 inch, while lighter but still beneficial rainfall reaches eastern Washington, the Idaho Panhandle and portions of northern California. Colder air will also lower snow levels to around 7,000 feet at times in the northern Washington Cascades, allowing snow to fall across the highest peaks. Travel across the mountain passes will remain unaffected. Temperatures will run 10-20 degrees below normal. While this rain may not completely end the fire season, it should provide meaningful relief, slow fire activity and help crews working on ongoing wildfires🌧️❄️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
Look west after sunset on September 1 for a meeting long in the making: the Evening Star beside the heart of the Maiden.

On September 1, Venus draws up alongside Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, in a close conjunction low in the west-southwest. Venus dominates the scene, gleaming brighter than any star in the sky, while Spica shines steadily just beside it. Though they appear as neighbours, Spica is a blue-white pair of giant stars far beyond our solar system, radiating thousands of times more light than the Sun.

🔭 The pairing sits low, so find an open western horizon and look about 45 minutes after sunset. A binocular brings both into one field. This is a fleeting view: within days, Spica fades into the twilight while Venus presses on, growing brighter toward a dazzling peak later in September 🌟✨

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: DOLLY REMNANTS HOLDING TOGETHER🌀the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly are holding together fairly well about 250 miles east of the Leeward Islands! There has been a recent flare-up of thunderstorms associated with the system, and while it looks fairly impressive on satellite, much of this convection is being sheared away from the main center of the remnant low. The remnants will continue moving west to west-northwest through the weekend and into early next week, potentially approaching the Bahamas, Florida, and possibly the eastern Gulf. As the system moves farther west, wind shear is expected to gradually decrease, which could provide a more favorable environment for some redevelopment. However, a lot depends on whether Dolly’s remnants can remain organized and intact long enough to reach those more favorable conditions. There’s no need to be overly concerned at this point, but this is something that Florida, the Bahamas, and surrounding areas should continue to closely monitor over the next several days🌀👀

items.text: ARIZONA HABOOB⚠️a significant blowing dust threat is developing across parts of southern and central Arizona later today! Blowing Dust Advisories are in effect from 4PM through 8–9 PM MST, including parts of the Phoenix Southeast Valley, Queen Creek, Pinal County, Gila Bend, the Tucson Metro, western Pima County and the Tohono O'odham Nation. Scattered strong thunderstorms developing around Tucson are expected to produce 45-55 mph wind gusts, with outflow boundaries spreading west and northwest. These thunderstorm outflows could generate haboobs, large walls of blowing dust, capable of rapidly reducing visibility. Visibility within areas of blowing dust could fall to 1/4 mile or less, with localized near-zero visibility possible. The dust threat includes stretches of I-10, I-8 and I-19, so travel could become dangerous very quickly. Never attempt to drive through a haboob. If blowing dust overtakes you on the roadway, pull completely off the road as far as possible, place the vehicle in park, turn off your lights and keep your foot off the brake pedal⚠️

items.text: ARIZONA FLOOD WATCH⚠️⛈️a widespread flash flood threat is developing across much of Arizona this weekend, with Flood Watches covering the Phoenix and Tucson Metros, Gila and Pinal counties, much of Maricopa and Yavapai counties, and parts of southeastern Arizona. The Flood Watch begins at 11 AM MST today around Tucson and continues through late Sunday night. For Phoenix, Yavapai County, northern Gila County, and the Oak Creek and Sycamore Canyon areas, the watch is in effect from this afternoon through late tonight. Increasing monsoonal moisture, atmospheric instability, and an approaching weather system will support scattered thunderstorms capable of producing very heavy rainfall. The strongest storms could generate rainfall rates exceeding 1 inch per hour, with isolated totals of 1-3 inches possible. Training thunderstorms may produce localized rainfall amounts over 2 inches around south-central Arizona. Flash flooding could quickly develop in normally dry washes, creeks, roadway dips, low-water crossings, urban areas, slot canyons, swimming holes, and recently burned areas⛈️

items.author: ericsnitilwx
items.text:
FOOLS' FALL: This Tuesday marks not only the start of the new month of September but the new meteorological season of fall. For those hoping this shift would bring more pumpkin spice weather, it ain't happening. At least not yet. The pattern next week will feature a pronounced ridge of high pressure nudging into the southeast United States. Heat and humidity will be the name of the game for many. 

For WNY, we'll find ourselves along the periphery of this ridge. This is often an area of active weather as opportunistic thunderstorms tap into the edge of that warm, unstable air. This will likely set the stage for multiple rounds of rain and thunderstorms next week. Wednesday continues to look like the day of most interest with regard to severe weather potential, something we'll take a day at a time. 

Regardless, it's going to get humid and very much feel like summer. No matter what the calendar says.

items.author: GulfCoastUpdates
items.text:
Have you ever heard of the “Brown Ocean Effect”?

FIVE YEARS AGO, Hurricane #Ida provided a striking example of this phenomenon.

After a hurricane makes landfall, it typically begins weakening rapidly as it loses access to the warm ocean water that provides its heat and moisture.

But under certain conditions, that weakening can happen much more slowly.

The Brown Ocean Effect occurs when extremely warm, saturated land — particularly wetlands, marshes and swampy areas, can continue supplying a tropical cyclone with significant heat and moisture after it moves inland.

This image of Hurricane Ida illustrates just how remarkable its inland strength was. Ida was still producing high end Category 3 intensity with winds of around 125 mph well after crossing the #Louisiana coastline.
